reading.body:
Hakeem Jeffries received at least $33,000 from AI company and AI-focused political committees between June 2025 and August 2026, alongside recorded votes on four bills.

The contributions come from a narrow set of donors: Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, Google, Meta, and Intel. Amazon gave twice, Microsoft twice, Oracle twice. The amounts are small and repeated rather than large and one-off, which is the pattern of routine committee giving rather than a single transaction tied to a single vote. The dates interleave with the votes rather than clustering around them.

The votes are all procedural. Each is a Yea on a motion to suspend the rules and pass, which is the fast-track route used for bills with broad support. The data does not record what any of the four bills, H.R. 7757, H.R. 5764, H.R. 1770, or S. 146, actually contains. Nothing here establishes that any contribution bought any vote, and the page states plainly that placement in date order is not a claim of causation.

What this record does not cover is as important as what it does. It holds no committee assignments, no sponsored bills, no statements, and no positions on data centers, transmission lines, or power procurement, which are where AI policy meets physical constraint. The money is from chipmakers and cloud providers, the companies whose buildout depends on those constraints, but the record shows only that they gave and that he voted. It cannot tell a reader what Jeffries thinks about the grid, and it should not be read as if it could.
